precepts.text: Thou shalt not suffer a witch to live.
precepts.point: And I will come near to you to judgment; and I will be a swift witness against the sorcerers.

note.label: We Are Born in Babylon

precepts.why:
“And I will come near to you to judgment; and I will be a swift witness against the sorcerers”. That is what we wanted to get to. The law already said what God thinks of sorcery: “Thou shalt not suffer a witch to live.”

Look at what our people are doing. Growing numbers of black women in Maryland and across the nation are leaving church worship for what they call ancient forms of spiritual contact. Some call it witchcraft, a term they accept and embrace, offering prayers to spirits and deities like Oshun. More than two hundred witches gathered at a convention in Baltimore. They grew up Christian, Baptist, Episcopal, a grandfather a preacher, a father a deacon, and now they call themselves witches. God said he is going to be a swift witness against the sorcerers.

A sister who used crystals testified that instead of healing you, it entices you and traps you into depending on it for every little thing; it is like a placebo effect. So brothers, be careful. Sisters come in with these crystals and say, oh no, it’s just spirituality. It is witchcraft. Don’t fall for it, or you are going to have demons all up in your house.

precepts.text: Ye shall not afflict any widow, or fatherless child. If thou afflict them in any wise, and they cry at all unto me, I will surely hear their cry; and my wrath shall wax hot, and I will kill you with the sword; and your wives shall be widows, and your children fatherless.
precepts.point: The widow, and the fatherless.

note.label: We Are Born in Babylon

precepts.why:
“and against those that oppress the hireling in his wages, the widow, and the fatherless”. The law on the widow and the fatherless is heavy: “Ye shall not afflict any widow, or fatherless child. If thou afflict them in any wise, and they cry at all unto me, I will surely hear their cry”.

“And my wrath shall wax hot, and I will kill you with the sword; and your wives shall be widows, and your children fatherless.” Damn. Whoever afflicts the widow and the fatherless, God makes his own wife a widow and his own children fatherless.

Then Malachi finishes: “For I am the Lord, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed.” The same God who wrote these laws has not changed, and he still judges the sorcerers, the adulterers, the false swearers and the oppressors. And because he changes not, the sons of Jacob are not consumed. That is why we are still in existence today, the twelve tribes.

precepts.text: Thou shalt not revile the gods nor curse the ruler of thy people; the gods and the rulers are the same men.
precepts.point: I have said ye are gods, and all of you are children of the most High, and he meant it; but ye shall die like men, like the heathen, for the darkness we walked in, which is why we cannot afford an inferiority complex.

note.label: The Superiority of the Chosen People

precepts.why:
“God standeth in the congregation of the mighty; he judgeth among the gods.” Who are the gods he judges among? The law answers it: “Thou shalt not revile the gods, nor curse the ruler of thy people.”

The gods and the ruler of thy people are the same men. The gods are our leaders, our judges. God always moved through the leadership of our forefathers: through Moses, through Aaron, through the captains and the officers. The spirit of the Lord would move and judge us through the leaders that were acting and moving correctly in that time.

So when the psalm says he judgeth among the gods, it is referring to our leaders, the men of Israel. That is why the psalm can go on to say “all the foundations of the earth are out of course”: when our leadership walked on in darkness and Israel went into sin, the world went out of order, because its rightful heirs and rulers are not in their proper place.

And that is why the Lord could say “Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High.” It was not a term of endearment; he meant it. The men of the children of Israel are gods, and because of that we cannot afford low self-esteem or an inferiority complex.

precepts.text: Steal an ox and you restore five oxen: the whole chapter restrains covetousness, like a speeding ticket raising your insurance. If a man entice a maid that is not betrothed, he coveted her behind her father's back, broke the tenth commandment, and the father can refuse him. Dinah was spoken to sweetly, not raped, and her brothers still would not give her. No backdoor marriages will be approved; if a sister has to be snatched out and sit with that scarlet letter, it is better than being tied to a man who went behind her father's back.
precepts.point: Moses bowed and said, if I have found grace, go among us, for it is a stiffnecked people, and pardon our iniquity and take us for thine inheritance. Stiffnecked then, the same hard heads today. The elect are the men and women who fit within the escape he created; do not get pulled off your game by slick talk.

note.label: The Divine Orchestration and Purpose of the People You Encounter

precepts.why:
Exodus 22 is the law put in place for those that wanted to do evil, and it is proper. The whole chapter is about putting restraints on covetousness. It is not telling you how you are supposed to move. It is like a speeding ticket: your insurance goes way up, and that is the consequence of breaking the original law. Drive the damn speed limit.

“If a man shall steal an ox, or a sheep, and kill it, or sell it; he shall restore five oxen for an ox, and four sheep for a sheep.” That is covetousness: you coveted thy neighbour's ox, exactly what Exodus 20:17 forbids. If you do, you pay for the one you stole and give him five oxen for it.

“And if a man entice a maid that is not betrothed, and lie with her, he shall surely endow her to be his wife.” The maid belongs to her father. To entice her means you coveted to get her; you did it behind the father's back, in deceit. You broke the tenth commandment, “nor any thing that is thy neighbour’s.” You lured her away from her father, and you are going to try to tell me that is righteous? You are a damn fool. And a woman that has no wisdom will follow that and pay for the judgment.

Verse 17 kills it: “If her father utterly refuse to give her unto him, he shall pay money according to the dowry of virgins.” The father said hell no. Even though you enticed her, you are not taking her. That is what happened with Dinah: she was enticed, spoken to sweetly and kindly; she was not raped. Even though he wanted to marry her, her brothers said no, snatched her out of that house, and she had to sit there defiled.

That should be a warning to you women. No backdoor marriages will be approved, period. If we have to snatch you out, and you have to sit with that scarlet letter knowing you were defiled, that is better than being tied up with somebody that means you pure evil. How could you even respect a man who went behind your father's back, your protection's back? This is the guilty that Exodus 34:7 says the Lord will by no means clear.

precepts.text: Because he hath sinned, and is guilty, he shall restore that which he took violently away, or the thing which he hath deceitfully gotten, or that about which he hath sworn falsely; he shall restore it in the principal, and shall add the fifth part more thereto, and give it unto him to whom it appertaineth. The recent matter was deceit: the fathers and leadership knew nothing until her sister discovered it, and they still were not going to say anything. You do not get the daughter and you still pay the fathers; that is why judgment goes forward, so no sister is beguiled by a brother claiming Exodus 22:16.
precepts.point: A sixth grader in the South stood up and put me on blast for a nasty note, and a sister in the world corrected an Israelite with a Bible in his hand, but grown women in the truth let men talk them out of their drawers and call it love.

note.label: The Vantage Point of the Elders: the Fathers Have Spoken

precepts.why:
Exodus 22:17: “If her father utterly refuse to give her unto him, he shall pay money according to the dowry of virgins”. He has to pay, but he still is not getting the daughter. Somebody might say, he paid, so he gets to take her. Leviticus 6 shows the principle: “Then it shall be, because he hath sinned, and is guilty, that he shall restore that which he took violently away”.

Took violently away. To entice that daughter against her father's wishes is to violate him, and violation is violence. That is the same reason a man who steals an ox must “restore five oxen for an ox”: the owner was violated, and restitution is paid for the violent act against him.

“or the thing which he hath deceitfully gotten”. The recent matter was deceit. Her fathers didn't know anything about it, the leadership didn't know anything about it, nobody knew until her sister discovered it, and they still weren't going to say anything. How are you going to come up later saying, here's the law?

“Or all that about which he hath sworn falsely; he shall even restore it in the principal, and shall add the fifth part more thereto, and give it unto him to whom it appertaineth, in the day of his trespass offering”. The principal is the actual thing taken, and the fifth part is added on top. So you are not getting the daughter, and you still have to pay the fathers. That is why the judgment goes forward: we will not leave that kind of example for the rest of the sisters, to be beguiled by a wicked brother who says we're applying Exodus 22:16. That's a damn lie.

precepts.text: The Pharisees tempted him with Moses' writing of divorcement, Deuteronomy 24, and Christ took them back to the beginning: he which made them made them male and female, and they twain shall be one flesh; what God hath joined together, let not man put asunder. God did not join backdoor marriages. Moses, because of the hardness of your hearts, suffered you to put away your wives, but from the beginning it was not so. Those are failsafe laws to keep negroes from going all the way wicked; you are not supposed to be in failure for them to come up, and quoting one after you went off does not make you righteous.
precepts.point: A sixth grader in the South stood up and put me on blast for a nasty note, and a sister in the world corrected an Israelite with a Bible in his hand, but grown women in the truth let men talk them out of their drawers and call it love.

note.label: The Vantage Point of the Elders: the Fathers Have Spoken

precepts.why:
The Pharisees came to Christ “tempting him, and saying unto him, Is it lawful for a man to put away his wife for every cause?” They were trying to use Moses' law, the writing of divorcement in Deuteronomy 24. Christ took them back to the beginning: “Have ye not read, that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female, And said, For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh?” From the beginning there was no such thing as divorce. What are you talking about, quoting Moses? It's the same as a negro trying to quote Exodus 22:16.

“Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder”. God did not put these backdoor marriages together. That's why love worketh no ill to his neighbour: you will not do evil and call yourself love. You don't love anything but your own lust.

“Why did Moses then command to give a writing of divorcement, and to put her away? He saith unto them, Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so”. The only reason Moses had to bring in that negro-proof law is that we were hard-headed and gave Moses hell. It is a failsafe law, a kind of bylaw to keep us from going all the way wicked. You are not supposed to be in failure at all for it even to come up, and quoting one after you went off and did wrong does not make you righteous.

That is covering violence with the garment: “for one covereth violence with his garment, saith the Lord of hosts: therefore take heed to your spirit, that ye deal not treacherously”. The Pharisees enlarged the borders of their garments, and the fringes represent the laws. A man who deceived to get a sister and then gives her a so-called law from the Bible is covering his violation with the law. Sisters and brothers, watch yourselves, hold yourselves in the diligence of the scriptures, and stop playing games.

precepts.text: Christ came not to destroy the law or the prophets but to fulfil; not one jot or tittle passes from the law till all be fulfilled.
precepts.point: If a man steal an ox or a sheep and kill it or sell it, he restores five oxen for an ox and four sheep for a sheep. We are in a different situation where we do not keep oxen and sheep, but the principle of restitution still applies among brothers and sisters in the body: if something is stolen, the law written here governs the payback. Do not be stealing.

note.label: Exodus 22: The Civil Laws of Restitution

precepts.why:
“Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil. For verily I say unto you, Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled.”

The law of restitution did not pass. We are in a different situation, where we do not keep oxen and sheep, but the principle still applies among brothers and sisters in the body: if something is stolen, the law written here governs the payback, five for an ox and four for a sheep. Do not be stealing.

precepts.text: An oath for confirmation is to men an end of all strife; God, willing to shew unto the heirs of promise the immutability of his counsel, confirmed it by an oath.
precepts.point: Paul uses this civil law to show how the Most High is unchangeable. An oath for confirmation is the end of all strife; God confirmed his counsel by an oath, and by two immutable things, that it is impossible for God to lie and that he will not take back what went out of his mouth, we have strong consolation. The same way, once the oath of this law is applied, the matter is over.

note.label: Exodus 22: The Civil Laws of Restitution

precepts.why:
When a beast left with a neighbour dies or is hurt or driven away with no man seeing it, “an oath of the Lord be between them both”. In layman’s terms he swears: I did not take the stuff, I did not set you up, I do not know where it is. Paul explains why that ends it: “For men verily swear by the greater: and an oath for confirmation is to them an end of all strife.” The owner accepts the oath and the matter ends there; it is not to be spoken of again.

Paul uses this civil law to show how the Most High is unchangeable: “Wherein God, willing more abundantly to shew unto the heirs of promise the immutability of his counsel, confirmed it by an oath: That by two immutable things, in which it was impossible for God to lie, we might have a strong consolation, who have fled for refuge to lay hold upon the hope set before us”. The two immutable things are that it is impossible for God to lie, and that he will not take back what went out of his mouth.

God confirmed his counsel by an oath, and that is the end of all strife for the heirs of promise. The same way, once the oath of this law is applied, the matter is over.

precepts.text: Marrying off the daughter was the father's weighty matter; she was given to a man of understanding.
precepts.point: The proper channel was that the father married off the daughter. To marry thy daughter is to perform a weighty matter, for the father gives her over to that man for the rest of her life and is out of all watching over her; so she is to be given to a man of understanding, one keeping the commandments as a wise man. In our own land the daughter went from her father's house to a husband's house with the blessing of the father.

note.label: Exodus 22: The Civil Laws of Restitution

precepts.why:
If a man entice a maid that is not betrothed and lie with her, “he shall surely endow her to be his wife”; he has to sign the papers. He is at fault for not going through the proper channels of marriage, and she is at fault for being enticed and laying down.

The proper channel was that the father married off the daughter: “Marry thy daughter, and so shalt thou have performed a weighty matter: but give her to a man of understanding.” It is a weighty matter because the father gives her over to that man for the rest of her life and is out of all watching over her. So she is to be given to a man of understanding, one keeping the commandments as a wise man.

In our own land the daughter went from her father’s house to a husband’s house with the blessing of the father. Enticement goes around all of that.

precepts.text: Shechem offered never so much dowry and gift for Dinah; the dowry stood even where the union was wrong.
precepts.point: The dowry of virgins was fifty shekels of silver, paid by the man who laid hold on a damsel not betrothed, and she became his wife whom he could not put away all his days. And if a husband afterward brought up an evil name upon a virgin of Israel, saying he found her not a maid, the tokens of her virginity, the cloth from the bedchamber her father kept, were spread before the elders; the man was chastised and amerced in an hundred shekels of silver for the false report.

note.label: Exodus 22: The Civil Laws of Restitution

precepts.why:
“If her father utterly refuse to give her unto him, he shall pay money according to the dowry of virgins.” The father does not agree with the backdoor marriage, and the man still pays. Genesis 34 gives the example with Dinah: “And Shechem said unto her father and unto her brethren, Let me find grace in your eyes, and what ye shall say unto me I will give. Ask me never so much dowry and gift, and I will give according as ye shall say unto me: but give me the damsel to wife.”

Shechem and his father Hamor begged Jacob for her and offered never so much dowry. Shechem understood the union was not supposed to take place, the Hebrews with the Hamites, and the dowry stood even where the union was wrong.

precepts.text: The man that lay with a damsel not betrothed gave her father fifty shekels of silver, and she became his wife; that is the dowry of virgins.
precepts.point: The dowry of virgins was fifty shekels of silver, paid by the man who laid hold on a damsel not betrothed, and she became his wife whom he could not put away all his days. And if a husband afterward brought up an evil name upon a virgin of Israel, saying he found her not a maid, the tokens of her virginity, the cloth from the bedchamber her father kept, were spread before the elders; the man was chastised and amerced in an hundred shekels of silver for the false report.

note.label: Exodus 22: The Civil Laws of Restitution

precepts.why:
What was the dowry of virgins? “If a man find a damsel that is a virgin, which is not betrothed, and lay hold on her, and lie with her, and they be found; Then the man that lay with her shall give unto the damsel’s father fifty shekels of silver, and she shall be his wife; because he hath humbled her, he may not put her away all his days.”

The dowry of virgins was fifty shekels of silver, paid to her father by the man who laid hold on a damsel not betrothed. She became his wife, and because he humbled her, he could not put her away all his days.

precepts.text: The tokens of virginity were spread before the elders, and the man that brought up an evil name on a virgin of Israel was amerced in an hundred shekels of silver.
precepts.point: The dowry of virgins was fifty shekels of silver, paid by the man who laid hold on a damsel not betrothed, and she became his wife whom he could not put away all his days. And if a husband afterward brought up an evil name upon a virgin of Israel, saying he found her not a maid, the tokens of her virginity, the cloth from the bedchamber her father kept, were spread before the elders; the man was chastised and amerced in an hundred shekels of silver for the false report.

note.label: Exodus 22: The Civil Laws of Restitution

precepts.why:
The dowry of virgins went with proof of virginity. If a husband afterward brought up an evil name upon his wife, her father answered before the elders: “he hath given occasions of speech against her, saying, I found not thy daughter a maid; and yet these are the tokens of my daughter’s virginity. And they shall spread the cloth before the elders of the city.” The tokens were the cloth from the bedchamber, which her father kept.

“And the elders of that city shall take that man and chastise him; And they shall amerce him in an hundred shekels of silver, and give them unto the father of the damsel, because he hath brought up an evil name upon a virgin of Israel: and she shall be his wife; he may not put her away all his days.” For the false report the man was chastised and amerced in an hundred shekels of silver, and still could not put her away.

precepts.text: If thy brother be waxen poor, though he be a stranger or a sojourner, relieve him; take no usury of him, and lend him not thy victuals for increase.
precepts.point: This is twofold, and first and foremost the stranger is your brother from a different area, our own people. Leviticus 25 shows it: if thy brother be waxen poor, though he be a stranger or a sojourner, sojourn meaning travel, thou shalt relieve him that he may live with thee. A brother of another tribe who falls on hard times and travels down to live with you is that stranger; neither vex him nor oppress him, for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt.

note.label: Exodus 22: The Civil Laws of Restitution

precepts.why:
This is twofold, and first and foremost the stranger is your brother from a different area, our own people. Leviticus 25 shows it: “And if thy brother be waxen poor, and fallen in decay with thee; then thou shalt relieve him: yea, though he be a stranger, or a sojourner; that he may live with thee.” Thy brother is called a stranger or a sojourner, and sojourn means travel. A brother of another tribe who falls on hard times and travels down to live with you is that stranger.

How he is to be treated: “Take thou no usury of him, or increase: but fear thy God; that thy brother may live with thee. Thou shalt not give him thy money upon usury, nor lend him thy victuals for increase.” Neither vex him nor oppress him, “for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt.”

precepts.text: They know not, neither will they understand; I have said, Ye are gods, and all of you are children of the Most High.
precepts.point: Acts 23 is the example: when Paul spoke against the high priest, they that stood by said, Revilest thou God's high priest? And Paul answered, I wist not, brethren, that he was the high priest: for it is written, Thou shalt not speak evil of the ruler of thy people, quoting this very verse.

note.label: Exodus 22: The Civil Laws of Restitution

precepts.why:
“Thou shalt not revile the gods” means do not hate or speak evil of your leaders. The word gods here is the leaders over you. The Most High says in the psalm, “I have said, Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High”, speaking of us.

The psalm says of them, “They know not, neither will they understand; they walk on in darkness: all the foundations of the earth are out of course.” Still they are called gods, children of the Most High, and the law says not to revile them, nor curse the ruler of thy people.

precepts.text: Paul, rebuked for reviling God's high priest, cited this law: it is written, Thou shalt not speak evil of the ruler of thy people.
precepts.point: Acts 23 is the example: when Paul spoke against the high priest, they that stood by said, Revilest thou God's high priest? And Paul answered, I wist not, brethren, that he was the high priest: for it is written, Thou shalt not speak evil of the ruler of thy people, quoting this very verse.

note.label: Exodus 22: The Civil Laws of Restitution

precepts.why:
Acts 23 is the example. Paul stood before the council, and “the high priest Ananias commanded them that stood by him to smite him on the mouth. Then said Paul unto him, God shall smite thee, thou whited wall: for sittest thou to judge me after the law, and commandest me to be smitten contrary to the law?”

“And they that stood by said, Revilest thou God’s high priest? Then said Paul, I wist not, brethren, that he was the high priest: for it is written, Thou shalt not speak evil of the ruler of thy people.” Paul quoted this very verse. Reviling the gods and cursing the ruler of thy people is speaking evil of the ruler, and Paul owned the law the moment he knew who he had spoken to.

precepts.text: That which dieth of itself is given to the stranger in thy gates or sold to an alien; thou art an holy people unto the Lord thy God.
precepts.point: Always get the context of the law, because sometimes the stranger is your brother and sometimes it is literally the other nations. Deuteronomy 14:21 doubles this law: that which dieth of itself thou shalt give unto the stranger that is in thy gates, or sell it unto an alien, for thou art an holy people unto the Lord thy God. Cast the torn flesh to the other nations; ye shall not eat it, because ye are holy people.

note.label: Exodus 22: The Civil Laws of Restitution

precepts.why:
“And ye shall be holy men unto me: neither shall ye eat any flesh that is torn of beasts in the field; ye shall cast it to the dogs.” This is twofold, and the dogs are the strangers of other nations, the aliens and foreigners. Deuteronomy 14:21 doubles the law and names them: “Ye shall not eat of any thing that dieth of itself: thou shalt give it unto the stranger that is in thy gates, that he may eat it; or thou mayest sell it unto an alien: for thou art an holy people unto the Lord thy God.”

Always get the context of the law, because sometimes the stranger is your brother and sometimes it is literally the other nations. Here it is the other nations: cast the torn flesh to them, give it to the stranger in thy gates or sell it to an alien. Ye shall not eat it, because ye are holy people unto the Lord thy God.

precepts.text: Five oxen for an ox and four sheep for a sheep; the thief restored the principal many times over.
precepts.point: Stealing was not a sin unto death, but the Lord made the restitution heavy so you would never commit it again. It goes back to the commandment, thou shalt not steal, and to the civil law where an ox was restored fivefold and a sheep fourfold.

note.label: Leviticus 6: The Trespass Offering and the Fire That Shall Never Go Out

precepts.why:
The civil law made the thief restore many times over: “If a man shall steal an ox, or a sheep, and kill it, or sell it; he shall restore five oxen for an ox, and four sheep for a sheep.”

That is the same principle as restoring it in the principal and adding the fifth part thereto: the value of what was taken had to be given back, with more added on top. A sorry would not settle it with the Lord; you could end up in debt for years over sticky fingers.

Stealing was not a sin unto death, but the Lord made the restitution heavy so you would never commit it again.

precepts.text: Thou shalt neither vex a stranger nor oppress him, for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt.
precepts.point: The bondmen laws show the contrast in how the word stranger is used. The bondmen and bondmaids were to be of the heathen round about, and in that context the children of the strangers sojourning among you are the heathen, a possession and an inheritance; but over your brethren the children of Israel ye shall not rule with rigour. Then the sojourner or stranger that waxeth rich by thee returns to the Israelite stranger, for the bondservant of the heathen did not wax rich.

note.label: Leviticus 19: Ye Shall Be Holy, for I the Lord Your God Am Holy

precepts.why:
“Thou shalt neither vex a stranger, nor oppress him: for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt.” The same law is given again in Leviticus 19:33-34 with the same reason: “ye were strangers in the land of Egypt.”

Israel knew what it was to sojourn in a land that was not their allotment. So the stranger dwelling with you is to be as one born among you, and you are to love him as yourself, not vex him.

precepts.text: If thou lend money to any of my people that is poor by thee, thou shalt not be to him as an usurer.
precepts.point: The same law was already read in Exodus: if thou lend money to any of my people that is poor by thee, thou shalt not be to him as an usurer.

note.label: Deuteronomy 23: Who May Enter the Congregation and the Holy Camp

precepts.why:
The same law was already read in Exodus: “If thou lend money to any of my people that is poor by thee, thou shalt not be to him as an usurer, neither shalt thou lay upon him usury.”

When you read the definition of usury, that is interest. Thou shalt not lend upon usury to thy brother, usury of money, of victuals, of any thing: we are not to charge interest to each other when we loan each other anything. Exodus and Deuteronomy are one law here, and the brother that is poor by thee is not to be treated as an usurer treats him.

precepts.text: If thou take thy neighbour's raiment to pledge, deliver it by that the sun goeth down, for that is his covering only.
precepts.point: The history shows how wicked we were to each other: Israel laid themselves down upon clothes laid to pledge by every altar, stacking up people's raiment like pallets and drinking the wine of the condemned in the house of their god, instead of returning the pledge before the sun went down as righteousness. That is why the Lord was judging us.

note.label: Deuteronomy 24: Divorcement, Pledges, and Mercy to the Poor

precepts.why:
The law of the poor man's pledge was already given: “If thou at all take thy neighbour’s raiment to pledge, thou shalt deliver it unto him by that the sun goeth down: For that is his covering only, it is his raiment for his skin: wherein shall he sleep? and it shall come to pass, when he crieth unto me, that I will hear; for I am gracious.”

That is the same word as “In any case thou shalt deliver him the pledge again when the sun goeth down, that he may sleep in his own raiment, and bless thee”. His raiment is his covering only; keep it overnight and he has nothing to sleep in, and when he crieth unto the Most High, he will hear, for he is gracious. Return it by sundown and he blesses thee instead, and it shall be righteousness unto thee before the Lord thy God.

precepts.text: Suffer not a witch to live; such practices are not Israel's custom.
precepts.point: The last straw for Saul was seeking that familiar spirit. Through Samuel the Most High told him he would join him the next day. The difference is that Samuel died righteously.

note.label: 1 Chronicles 10: The Death of Saul

precepts.why:
“Thou shalt not suffer a witch to live.” Witchcraft and consulting familiar spirits are not Israel's custom. The law does not even suffer the witch to live among the people.

That is what Saul turned to. The king who should have kept the word of the Lord went seeking counsel from a woman that the law says not to suffer to live, and he “enquired not of the Lord: therefore he slew him, and turned the kingdom unto David the son of Jesse.”

points: But if her father utterly refuse to give her unto him: the father has a choice. The father can refuse even then. A lot of times we do not understand the amount of power the father has in the home, and nothing changes when that father is a husband: the same power he has over his children is the power he has over his wife. So where is there room for disrespect? There is not.

points: If a man entice a maid and lie with her he shall endow her to be his wife: with sex comes obligation, and anything other than that is fornication.

points: If a thief be found breaking up, and be smitten that he die, there shall no blood be shed for him. The castle doctrine and self-defense laws came from our records. We do not advocate violence on any level and are not in a weapons race, but the nation needs a level of preservation: if someone comes to attack you, you have the right to protect yourself by any means necessary, and make sure they do not do it to anyone else. Do not go looking for anybody; get into this Bible and build your families.

Luke 22:36: he that hath no sword, let him sell his garment, and buy one. Christ said it because he was going off the scene and the disciples would be left to defend the gospel and would be attacked. That is the Bible, and I am not sorry about anything the Bible says.

The hard times and the destruction of our nation have created strong men. Surely oppression maketh a wise man mad, not a dumb man: wise enough to organize, to teach his children and his nation, and to get them up out of the mud. And because of that they come against us, and we are not supposed to lay down and let them run over us.

note.label: The Vantage Point of the Elders & Fathers: the Children Are Listening

points: Chapter 20 is the ten commandments; from there through chapter 22 is wrongdoing. When a verse starts with if, something is already wrong: you did not listen to the law, and a civilized mandate has to keep you from being totally wicked. If a man shall steal an ox, he shall restore five oxen for an ox, because the owner was violated. Violence is violation; to entice a daughter behind her father's back is violence, and then to quote a scripture saying we are doing right is covering evil with the garment.

note.label: The Vantage Point of the Elders: the Fathers Have Spoken

points: If a man entice a maid that is not betrothed, and lie with her, he shall surely endow her to be his wife. That is what negroes run with through the schools. On Instagram to the world it is appropriate, because the girl in the street has no father or leadership, and the least a man can do is take her as his wife. But in here the sisters have fathers, and if her father utterly refuse to give her unto him, he shall pay money according to the dowry of virgins. Utterly refused means cursing, throwing things, grabbing the shotgun: yes, my daughter was dumb enough to lay with you, but I am not giving her to you, and she sits with the stain so she is closed the next time. He pays and still does not get her; Jacob, Simeon, and Levi took that risk with the surrounding nations rather than let Shechem keep Dinah.

note.label: The Vantage Point of the Elders: the Fathers Have Spoken

points: A thief restores five oxen for an ox and four sheep for a sheep, and if he has nothing he is sold for his theft.
Israel had courts of law for restitution, fire, trespass and goods held in trust.

note.label: Jubilee: The Year To Be Set Free

points: If a man steal an ox or a sheep and kill it or sell it, he restores five oxen for an ox and four sheep for a sheep. We are in a different situation where we do not keep oxen and sheep, but the principle of restitution still applies among brothers and sisters in the body: if something is stolen, the law written here governs the payback. Do not be stealing.

note.label: Exodus 22: The Civil Laws of Restitution

points: If a thief be found breaking up means breaking in. He entered your home and you defended yourself and he died: that is what is called self-defense today, and no blood is shed for him, meaning there is no judgment. The judgment was already passed in the breaking in.

note.label: Exodus 22: The Civil Laws of Restitution

points: If the sun be risen upon him, the thief got away, and there shall be blood shed for him means there shall be a judgment; then the verse gives the judgment. He makes full restitution, and if he have nothing he is sold for his theft: not sold into slavery, but into work servitude until he pays off the debt of what he stole.

note.label: Exodus 22: The Civil Laws of Restitution

points: If the theft be found in his hand alive, he restores double. Verse three covers the thief who already got rid of what he stole; verse four covers the one still holding it.

note.label: Exodus 22: The Civil Laws of Restitution

points: These are self-explanatory: if a man lets his beast feed in another man's field or vineyard, he makes restitution of the best of his own field and vineyard; and he that kindles a fire that consumes another man's corn surely makes restitution.

note.label: Exodus 22: The Civil Laws of Restitution

points: If a man deliver money or stuff to his neighbor to keep and it be stolen, the thief found pays double. If the thief be not found, the master of the house is brought unto the judges, to see whether he put his hand unto his neighbor's goods, whether he was part of a scheme to deceive the owner out of his goods.

note.label: Exodus 22: The Civil Laws of Restitution

points: For all manner of trespass, whether for ox, ass, sheep, raiment, or any lost thing, both parties come before the judges, and whom the judges condemn pays double unto his neighbor.

note.label: Exodus 22: The Civil Laws of Restitution

points: If a beast delivered to a neighbor to keep die or be hurt or driven away, no man seeing it, an oath of the Lord is between them both. In layman's terms he swears: I did not take the stuff, I did not set you up, I do not know where it is. The owner accepts the oath and the matter ends there; it is not to be spoken of again.

note.label: Exodus 22: The Civil Laws of Restitution

points: If the thing kept be stolen from him, he makes restitution; if it be torn in pieces, he brings it for witness and does not make it good.

note.label: Exodus 22: The Civil Laws of Restitution

points: If a man borrow ought of his neighbor, ought meaning anything, and it be hurt or die with the owner not present, he surely makes it good. You borrowed it, it got messed up, you owe the man.

note.label: Exodus 22: The Civil Laws of Restitution

points: But if the owner be with it, or if it be an hired thing, it came for its hire. If you came to plow a man's field for ten shekels with your own donkey and your donkey breaks his leg, you cannot expect the owner to pay for your own faulty equipment; the same as a business loan today, the property owner is not liable when your own equipment breaks down.

note.label: Exodus 22: The Civil Laws of Restitution

points: If a man entice a maid that is not betrothed and lie with her, he shall surely endow her to be his wife; he has to sign the papers. He is at fault for not going through the proper channels of marriage, and she is at fault for being enticed and laying down.

The dowry of virgins was fifty shekels of silver, paid by the man who laid hold on a damsel not betrothed, and she became his wife whom he could not put away all his days. And if a husband afterward brought up an evil name upon a virgin of Israel, saying he found her not a maid, the tokens of her virginity, the cloth from the bedchamber her father kept, were spread before the elders; the man was chastised and amerced in an hundred shekels of silver for the false report.

note.label: Exodus 22: The Civil Laws of Restitution

points: If her father utterly refuse to give her unto him, he does not agree with the backdoor marriage, the man still pays money according to the dowry of virgins. Genesis 34 gives the example with Dinah: Shechem and his father Hamor begged Jacob for her and offered never so much dowry, for Shechem understood the union was not supposed to take place, the Hebrews with the Hamites.

note.label: Exodus 22: The Civil Laws of Restitution

points: Thou shalt not suffer a witch to live: witchcraft goes into horoscopes, palm readings, and all things of that nature.

note.label: Exodus 22: The Civil Laws of Restitution

points: Whosoever lieth with a beast, bestiality, shall surely be put to death.

note.label: Exodus 22: The Civil Laws of Restitution

points: He that sacrificeth unto any god save unto the Lord only shall be utterly destroyed.

note.label: Exodus 22: The Civil Laws of Restitution

points: This is twofold, and first and foremost the stranger is your brother from a different area, our own people. Leviticus 25 shows it: if thy brother be waxen poor, though he be a stranger or a sojourner, sojourn meaning travel, thou shalt relieve him that he may live with thee. A brother of another tribe who falls on hard times and travels down to live with you is that stranger; neither vex him nor oppress him, for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt.

note.label: Exodus 22: The Civil Laws of Restitution

points: Ye shall not afflict any widow or fatherless child. A wife without a husband already has a hard life, and a son or daughter without a father the same; do not make their life harder than it already is.

note.label: Exodus 22: The Civil Laws of Restitution

points: If thou afflict them in any wise and they cry unto the Most High, he will surely hear their cry, and his wrath shall wax hot: he will kill you with the sword, and your own wives shall be widows and your children fatherless. That is the Lord's plain warning against mistreating those less fortunate.

note.label: Exodus 22: The Civil Laws of Restitution

points: Usury means interest. You cannot charge your brother or sister interest: if you lend twenty dollars, you get twenty dollars back, nothing more, nothing less; no little bit more off the top. This is the same law read in Leviticus 25:36-37.

note.label: Exodus 22: The Civil Laws of Restitution

points: If thou take thy neighbor's raiment to pledge, deliver it unto him by that the sun goeth down, for that is his covering only; wherein shall he sleep? The tunics and overcoats worn then were also sleeping garments to keep a man warm at night, especially the poor.

note.label: Exodus 22: The Civil Laws of Restitution

points: A well-off man does not have to work for you; this speaks of the less fortunate who extend their services for money and give what is most valuable to them, their raiment, as the pledge. If he cries unto the Most High, he will hear, for he is gracious.

note.label: Exodus 22: The Civil Laws of Restitution

points: Thou shalt not revile the gods means do not hate or speak evil of your leaders. The word gods here is the leaders over you: the Most High says in the psalm, I have said, Ye are gods, and all of you are children of the Most High, speaking of us.

Acts 23 is the example: when Paul spoke against the high priest, they that stood by said, Revilest thou God's high priest? And Paul answered, I wist not, brethren, that he was the high priest: for it is written, Thou shalt not speak evil of the ruler of thy people, quoting this very verse.

note.label: Exodus 22: The Civil Laws of Restitution

points: Thou shalt not delay to offer the first of thy ripe fruits and of thy liquors, and the firstborn of thy sons shalt thou give unto me. The firstborn sons that opened the matrix were consecrated unto the Lord, and the father redeemed them back from the priest with shekels.

note.label: Exodus 22: The Civil Laws of Restitution

points: Likewise with the oxen and the sheep: seven days the firstling stayed with his dam, his mother, and on the eighth day it was given. The Lord did not want it too young, taken as soon as it popped out; it had to be its appointed time with the mother, then brought to the priest.

note.label: Exodus 22: The Civil Laws of Restitution

points: Ye shall be holy men unto me: neither shall ye eat any flesh that is torn of beasts in the field; ye shall cast it to the dogs. This is twofold, and the dogs are the strangers of other nations, the aliens and foreigners.

Always get the context of the law, because sometimes the stranger is your brother and sometimes it is literally the other nations. Deuteronomy 14:21 doubles this law: that which dieth of itself thou shalt give unto the stranger that is in thy gates, or sell it unto an alien, for thou art an holy people unto the Lord thy God. Cast the torn flesh to the other nations; ye shall not eat it, because ye are holy people.
